title: Leading Effective Professional Learning Communities
author: Sadie McCleary
summary: Sadie McCleary of Teach Like a Champion describes a common failure in professional learning communities, where the lead and one enthusiastic teacher dominate while newer teachers hesitate and another checks out. Because teachers spend only about three hours a week on collaborative learning, she says that time must be used thoughtfully. The feedback her team gives most often after observing PLCs across the country is to use Means of Participation such as Everybody Writes, Turn and Talk and Cold Call with adults, so that every teacher is asked to contribute. She illustrates this with two videos from Fayette County Public Schools in Georgia. In a first-grade reading PLC the leader has everyone analyse exemplars independently at the start, and in an Algebra I technique session the facilitator moves from writing to pair talk to whole-group discussion to practice. Both give equal voice and model sequences that teachers can reuse in their own classrooms.
points: A typical PLC gives most airtime to the lead and the most experienced or enthusiastic teacher while newer or disengaged teachers drift.
Teachers average about three hours a week on collaborative learning, so facilitation quality is a high-leverage use of constrained time.
The most frequent coaching advice is to apply Means of Participation such as Everybody Writes, Turn and Talk and Cold Call to adults as well as students.
Starting a PLC with an independent task tied to teachers' own classrooms gives every participant an immediate way in regardless of experience.
A write, turn and talk, whole-group, practise sequence doubles as a model teachers can transfer to their own lessons.
quotes: Teachers’ time is our most valuable (and constrained) educational asset, so it’s important that this team is used thoughtfully.

Perhaps surprisingly, the piece of feedback we find ourselves giving the most is to intentionally use Means of Participation (e.g., Everybody Writes, Turn and Talk, Cold Call) with adults to ensure all teachers are asked to contribute, not just the teacher with the most experience and/or enthusiasm.
Right off the bat, all teachers in the PLC, regardless of their experience level, have an immediate opportunity to actively engage with the content.

Just like with our students, Lisa immediately signals that the PLC will be an active learning environment for all participants and she ensures that the learning task is directly tied to each of their classrooms.

This replicable sequence of Means of Participation similarly ensures that all teachers are active participants in their own learning AND provides a model for a sequence of activities that could be applied to classrooms.
Both of these PLC experiences from Fayette County ensure that there is greater voice equity and active participation than in the image at the top of this post.
